entry.title: Sparse-Stream Memory Networks: The Next Evolution in Efficient AI
entry.summary: The AI world has a memory problem. Modern language models like GPT and Claude achieve impressive results, but at a cost: quadratic complexity. Every new token must attend to every previous token, creating an O(n²) bottleneck that makes long-context processing prohibitively expensive. What if we could keep the intelligence but ditch the quadratic scaling? Enter Sparse-Stream Memory Networks (SSMN) — a revolutionary architecture that processes infinite sequences in linear time by replacing attention's "spotlight" with synaptic "ink." SSMN is part of the Memory-Native Neural Network (MNNN) family — a new class of architectures where memory isn't just storage, it's the computation itself. Transformers work by having each token "look at" all previous tokens to understand context. This is powerf…

entry.title: LLMs Aren’t What I Thought They Were
entry.summary:
I kept seeing LLM everywhere. At first, I assumed it was just another fancy name for ChatGPT — That assumption slowed everything down. In my head, an LLM was: a magical AI brain something only researchers build tightly coupled to one specific task That felt reasonable. “Large Language Model” sounds intimidating. But this mental model created friction: I didn’t know where it fit in an app I couldn’t tell what part I was actually using
Everything felt more complex than it needed to be The shift happened when I stopped thinking of LLMs as products infrastructure. An LLM is not ChatGPT. product built on top of an LLM. Models like GPT and Gemini power products such as ChatGPT, That single distinction changed how I thought about AI. At its core, an LLM is a system designed to do one thing extremely well: predict the next word. It doesn’t understand language the way humans do. That’s why it feels intelligent. Two things matter most. 1. “Large” means data, not size LLMs are trained on huge datasets — books, articles, websites — patterns of language. 2. They’re general-purpose Unlike traditional ML models built for one task, chat interfaces code assistants summarizers explainers The same engine — different products. This finally clicked when I thought about frontend tools. React isn’t a product. In the same way: LLMs aren’t apps they’re engines behind apps What you experience depends entirely on: the interface the constraints the instructions on top There is one more layer underneath all of this — Under the hood, LLMs work by repeatedly predicting the next word in a sequence. transformers — I didn’t need to understand transformers to use LLMs — LLMs felt intimidating because I misunderstood what they were. Once I saw them as powerful prediction engines, approachable.
